claims.text: The untreated starting material is an equiatomic or near-equiatomic HEA such as CoCrFeMnNi in a single-phase solid-solution state without added soft-metal phases.
Adding 3–5 at.% Ag during alloy synthesis can produce a uniform Ag distribution that remains capable of segregating to wear surfaces.
Standard melting, casting, and thermomechanical processing will ensure a homogeneous Ag-containing microstructure.
A 3–5 at.% Ag addition will induce an adaptive, continuous Ag-rich tribolayer during sliding.
The interfacial Ag-rich material will have a nanolamellar or film-like morphology.
Silver segregates from the alloy to the sliding interface under wear-induced stress.
Silver's relatively low melting point and high mobility promote its migration to the contact surface under sliding conditions.
Silver reaching the contact surface coalesces into a continuous tribolayer.
The Ag-rich tribolayer provides a low-shear-strength barrier between the contacting surfaces.
The low-shear Ag-rich layer reduces interfacial shear and therefore lowers the coefficient of friction.
The Ag-rich layer protects the harder HEA matrix from severe material removal and therefore lowers wear rate.
The host HEA's thermal stability will allow the Ag-rich tribolayer mechanism to remain effective from room temperature to about 600 °C.
Relative to the untreated alloy, Ag alloying will reduce coefficient of friction by an estimated 20–30% across the tested temperature range.
Relative to the untreated alloy, Ag alloying will reduce wear rate by about 40–50% across the tested temperature range.
The untreated HEA has higher friction and wear because it lacks a lubricious interfacial phase.
The mechanism will remain effective only at loads and sliding speeds that permit formation and maintenance of the Ag-rich tribolayer.
Extremely high temperatures or aggressive wear conditions may disrupt the continuity of the Ag-rich layer.
